chapters.title: Chapter 2: How Trade Wars Move Markets

lessons.title: The Transmission Channels: Currency, Commodities, and Capital Flows

children.text: None of the tariff announcements you read about in the news are fired directly at your Nifty portfolio. They arrive secondhand, through three channels: the rupee, commodities, and capital flows. Learn to read these three, and a trade war headline stops being noise and starts being a set of specific things to check.

When trade tension escalates, global capital tends to run toward the US dollar as a safe haven, which strengthens the Dollar Index (DXY) and weakens most other currencies against it, the rupee included. A weaker INR makes India's oil import bill costlier in rupee terms (India imports roughly 85% of the crude oil it consumes), pushes up imported inflation, and can spook the same FII flows that were already nervous. The RBI does not let the rupee move freely in either direction. It intervenes by selling dollars from its foreign exchange reserves to slow a sharp fall, or buying dollars to prevent excessive appreciation, aiming to manage volatility rather than defend a fixed level.

stats.label: India's Crude Oil Import Dependency
stats.context: Share of India's crude oil consumption met through imports, which is why rupee weakness directly raises the oil import bill

stats.label: RBI Forex Reserves
stats.context: Fluctuates with RBI intervention; among the largest reserve buffers of any emerging market, used to smooth rupee volatility

stats.label: Import Cover
stats.context: Roughly how many months of India's imports the forex reserves could fund if inflows stopped entirely, a standard measure of external stability

children.text: Trade wars move commodity prices in two opposite directions at once, and India sits exposed to both. Fear of slower global growth typically pulls industrial metals and crude oil prices down, since a trade war is expected to shrink global demand for everything from steel to shipping fuel. At the same time, the same risk-off mood that hits equities sends investors toward gold as a safe haven, pushing gold prices up. India is a major importer of both crude oil and gold, so a trade war can simultaneously cut India's oil import bill (a rare silver lining) while making its gold import bill, and the current account deficit, worse. Metals themselves can also be a direct target: steel and aluminum tariffs specifically raise or lower prices for Indian producers and users of those metals, depending on which side of the tariff wall they sit on.

body.text: A trade war is one of the few global shocks where India's two largest import bills, crude oil and gold, can move in opposite directions at the same time. Do not assume a trade war is automatically bad news for India's import bill; check oil and gold separately before drawing a conclusion.

markDefs.definition: SEBI formally reclassified Foreign Institutional Investors (FIIs) as Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs) in 2014. The two terms describe the same category of overseas investors in Indian securities and are still used interchangeably in market commentary and even on NSE/BSE data feeds.

children.text: Foreign investors are the marginal buyers and sellers who set the price at the edges of the Indian market. When trade war risk rises,

flows tend to reverse out of emerging markets, including India, toward perceived safety. You can watch this happen in near real time: India VIX (the volatility index) tends to spike, NSE/BSE provisional FII/DII data gets published daily after market close, and export-heavy, high-beta sectors usually move first and hardest, while defensive sectors like FMCG and utilities hold up comparatively better. Domestic Institutional Investors (DIIs), mutual funds and insurers largely, have increasingly offset FII selling in recent years, which is one reason Indian markets have sometimes shrugged off global trade war stress faster than they used to.

body.title: Which Channel Is Firing?
body.scenario: Overnight, the US announces a fresh round of tariffs on Chinese electronics. By the next morning in India, the Dollar Index has jumped, Brent crude has fallen 3% on demand-slowdown fears, gold has risen 1.5%, and India VIX has spiked 12%.
body.prompt: Which of the three transmission channels are active here, and what would you expect to check next for each one?
body.modelAnswer: All three are active at once, which is common in a sharp risk-off move. Currency: a stronger DXY typically pressures the rupee, so check USD/INR and whether the RBI is intervening. Commodities: falling crude is a modest positive for India's import bill, while rising gold reflects safe-haven demand and worsens the gold import bill, so the net commodity effect needs both legs checked, not just one. Capital flows: a India VIX spike of that size usually coincides with FII selling, so check the day's provisional FII/DII data once markets close, and watch whether export-heavy sectors are underperforming defensives, which would confirm capital flows are the dominant channel that day.

body.title: A Three-Channel Reading Framework
steps: Check the Dollar Index (DXY) and USD/INR: is the rupee under pressure, and is the RBI visibly intervening?
Check Brent crude and gold separately: they often move in opposite directions during a trade war and the net effect on India's import bill is not automatic
Check India VIX and the day's provisional FII/DII data on NSE/BSE: is foreign money actively leaving, or is domestic buying offsetting it?
Check which sectors are moving first: export-heavy and high-beta sectors moving before defensives is a sign capital flows are the dominant channel that day

body.text: A trade war never hits the Nifty directly. It hits the rupee, oil, gold, and foreign flows first, and the Nifty is what happens after those three channels finish arguing with each other.

points: Currency: trade war stress usually strengthens the dollar and weakens the rupee, raising India's oil import bill and inviting RBI intervention.
Commodities: crude oil and gold often move in opposite directions during a trade war, since one reflects growth fears and the other reflects safe-haven demand.

Capital flows: FII/FPI money tends to leave emerging markets, including India, during trade war stress, visible through India VIX spikes and daily FII/DII data, though DII buying has increasingly cushioned the impact.
These three channels usually move together, not in isolation, so reading a trade war headline means checking all three, not picking the one that confirms your first reaction.
